deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated parts. (A) In the upper middle is analytic work on counting primes. (B) In the margins and the lower half are continued-fraction / reduced-form computations for √N, N = 247–255, continuing the previous page (N = 243–246) and leading into the next page (255–260).

(A1) Top. '(N1)' and '(N2) = ½(½N1) + ⅔(⅓N1) + ⅘(⅕N1) &c.' I read 'N1' as a counting function of numbers with one prime factor up to N, so N1 ≈ π(N). '(1/p N1)' is that function evaluated at N/p. On this reading N2 is a count of numbers with two prime factors, expressed as Σ_p ((p−1)/p)·N1(N/p) over p = 2, 3, 5, …. The weights (p−1)/p are as written; their justification is not visible on the page.
- Inserting N1(y) ≈ y/log y gives the next line exactly: N/(4·log(½N)) + 2N/(9·log(⅓N)) [+ …].
- Check: ½·(½N)/log(N/2) = N/(4 log(N/2)) and ⅔·(⅓N)/log(N/3) = 2N/(9 log(N/3)).
- This connects with Gauss's known Nachlass work on the count of numbers with two prime factors (~ x log log x / log x).

(A2) 'φx + φ√x + φ∛x + &c.' and 'n/ln + √n/(½ln) + ∛n/(⅓ln) …'. Here φ is a prime-counting function, so Σ_k φ(x^{1/k}) counts prime powers. Inserting φ(y) ≈ y/log y gives Σ_k x^{1/k}/log(x^{1/k}) = Σ_k k·x^{1/k}/log x, which is what is written.

(A3) The inverse problem: find φ with x = φ(x) + ½φ(x²) + ⅓φ(x³) + … (written 'x = φx + ½φ(x²) + ⅓φ(x³) + (⅙φx⁶)').
- Formal power-series solution: φ(x) = Σ μ(n)/n·x^n = x − ½x² − ⅓x³ + 0·x⁴ − ⅕x⁵ + ⅙x⁶ − …
- The written trial series is 'x − ½xx − ⅓x³ + ¼x⁴'. Its first three coefficients are right.
- The bracketed '(⅙ φ x⁶)' looks like the check of the x⁶ coefficient: c6 + ½c3 + ⅓c2 + ⅙c1 = 0, which gives c6 = +1/6 (my reconstruction).

(A4) Substitution x = e^t with ψ(t) = φ(e^t). On the page: 'φx = ψt', '… = ψ l x', i.e. ψ = φ∘exp, φ = ψ∘log. The equation becomes e^t = ψ(t) + ½ψ(2t) + ⅓ψ(3t) + &c. The last line, e^t = ω(t) + ω(2t) + ω(3t) + &c., is the same inversion problem without the 1/n weights. Its formal solution is ω(t) = Σ μ(n)e^{nt}. This is Möbius-type inversion in additive (dilation) form. Note that the prime-counting application would need x^{1/n}, i.e. ψ(t/n), whereas Gauss writes x^n and nt; the step from one to the other is not carried out here.

(B) Continued fraction of √N, in Gauss's notation. With a0 = 15 = ⌊√N⌋, P1 = 15, Q0 = 1, Q1 = N − 225 and the recursion a_k = ⌊(15+P_k)/Q_k⌋, P_{k+1} = a_kQ_k − P_k, Q_{k+1} = (N − P_{k+1}²)/Q_k, Gauss lists Q_k with alternating sign and P_k as a superscript. These are the forms (±Q_k, P_k, ∓Q_{k+1}) of determinant N (same layout as the previous page's 243–246). All values below are verified by me.
- 253: Q = 1, 28, 3, 19, 12, 17, 9, 21, 4, 7, 12, 11 with P = 15, 13, 14, 5, 7, 10, 8, 13, 15, 13, 11, 11. The period is symmetric about P = 11 = P, so the period length is odd (21). Q = 11 divides 253 = 11·23.
- 255: 1, −30 (P = 15); the period is immediate. The next page lists the factorisations 1·30, 2·15, 3·10, 5·6.
- 254: principal cycle +1, −29(15), +2(14), −29, +1, with mirrored signs in the second column. Then a second, non-principal chain +17, −5(13), +22(12), −7(10), +19(11), +10(8), −11(12), +14, −17. Each step satisfies 254 − P² = Q·Q′ and P′ ≡ −P (mod Q): e.g. 254−169 = 17·5, 254−144 = 5·22, 254−100 = 22·7, 254−121 = 7·19, 254−64 = 19·10, 254−144 = 10·11, and implicitly 254−100 = 11·14, 254−16 = 14·17. This is a class enumeration for determinant 254.
- 252: 1, 27(15), 4(12), then symmetric. Second cycle 7(14), 8(10), 19(9), 9.
- 249: 1, 24(15), 7(9), 15(12), 16(3), 5(13), 21(12), 8(9), 3(15).
- 251: 1, 26(15), 5(11), 11(14), 17(8), 10(9), 13(11), 2(15).
- 247: 1, 22(15), 9(7), 14(11), 17(3), 3(14), 26(13); symmetric centre with 26 = 2·13 and 13 | 247.
- 248: 1, 23(15), 8(8), symmetric. Second cycle 8, 13(12), 4(14), summarised as '+1, −23, +8 / +4, −13, +8'.
- Unlabelled column: N = 250: 1, 25(15), 6(10), 9(14), 9(13), symmetric.
Purpose: enumerating cycles of reduced forms for consecutive positive determinants (class-number tables; cf. '4 Ordines' on the previous page). The symmetric points incidentally expose factors.
errors: The trial series 'x − ½xx − ⅓x³ + ¼x⁴' has a wrong x⁴ term if read as written. The correct inverse φ(x) = Σ μ(n)x^n/n has coefficient 0 for x⁴ (contributions c4 − ¼ + ¼ = 0). The ¼x⁴ (the exponent appears overwritten) may be a slip or a struck term. The heavy mark before ⅓x³ suggests correction activity.

In (N2) = Σ ((p−1)/p)·N1(N/p) the weights (p−1)/p are not justified on the page. A plain count of products of two primes would use Σ_p π(N/p) with a correction for double counting. Whether this is an error or a different definition of N2 cannot be decided from this page.

The weighted inversion x = Σ φ(x^n)/n uses powers x^n, whereas the prime-power count on the same page involves roots x^{1/n}. As written the formal problem is the dual; this is not an error, but the link is not made explicit.
All continued-fraction / form entries I checked (247–255, plus the second cycles of 248, 252, 254) are arithmetically correct.

results.what: Approximating a count of two-prime-factor numbers by Σ_p ((p−1)/p)·π(N/p) with π(y) ≈ y/log y, giving N/(4 log(N/2)) + 2N/(9 log(N/3)) + …
results.modern_name: Asymptotics of π_2(x) (semiprimes / numbers with two prime factors), Landau's π_k(x) ~ x(log log x)^{k−1}/((k−1)! log x)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Nachlass, reported in Werke X.1) and Landau 1900 for proof

results.what: Counting prime powers as Σ_k φ(x^{1/k}) with φ(y) ≈ y/log y, i.e. Σ k·x^{1/k}/log x
results.modern_name: Prime-power counting; relation of Riemann's Π(x) / Chebyshev-type sums to π(x)
results.usually_credited_to: Chebyshev (1848–50), Riemann (1859) for the weighted Π(x) = Σ π(x^{1/n})/n

results.what: Formal inversion of x = Σ (1/n)φ(x^n), solved termwise as φ(x) = x − ½x² − ⅓x³ − ⅕x⁵ + ⅙x⁶ …; transformed by x = e^t to e^t = Σ ψ(nt)/n and to e^t = Σ ω(nt)
results.modern_name: Möbius inversion (power-series / multiplicative-argument form); Riemann's inversion π(x) = Σ μ(n)Π(x^{1/n})/n is the analytic analogue
results.usually_credited_to: A. F. Möbius 1832 (series inversion); Riemann 1859 for the prime-counting application

results.what: Continued-fraction expansion of √N (cycles of reduced forms (±Q, P, ∓Q′) of determinant N) for N = 247–255, including non-principal cycles for 248, 252, 254
results.modern_name: Periodic continued fraction of √N / cycles of reduced indefinite binary quadratic forms; class-number tabulation
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange, Legendre; Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae arts. 183–205 and his class-number tables

deep.surprise_reason: The form-cycle tables are routine Gauss material (class tables for positive determinants). The analytic fragment is more interesting. It juxtaposes prime-power counting Σ φ(x^{1/k}) with a Möbius-type inversion of Σ φ(x^n)/n, solved by coefficients μ(n)/n, plus the dilation form e^t = Σ ω(nt). Together these foreshadow Riemann's π(x) = Σ μ(n)Π(x^{1/n})/n. However, Gauss's use of Möbius-type inversion is already known (counting irreducible polynomials mod p, ca. 1797), and his π_2(x) work is in Werke X. The page does not actually state the Riemann formula, and the trial series contains a slip. So this is a notable but modest unpublished detail.

checkable.asserts: φ(x) = Σ μ(n)x^n/n solves x = Σ φ(x^n)/n up to order 12.
The correct coefficients are 1, −½, −⅓, 0, −⅕, ⅙, so the x⁴ coefficient is 0, not ¼.
The √253 expansion behind Gauss's Q-list 1, 28, 3, 19, 12, 17, 9, 21, 4, 7, 12, 11 has odd period 21.
Gauss's (Q, P) table for 253 satisfies N − P² = Q·Q′ at every step.
The non-principal chain for determinant 254 (+17, −5, +22, −7, +19, +10, −11, +14, −17) consists of adjacent forms.
Gauss's 247 table is correct; the symmetric point reveals the factor 13.
The unlabelled bottom-right column is the √250 expansion.
The second cycles for 252 and 248 are correct.
